correctness.rationale: Back first reaches the universal target world Y and then every nonempty target world. In particular, by forth from X to a preimage of each target singleton, F(X)=Y. If the image of a source singleton contained two distinct atoms, back would lift their singleton worlds to two sets containing the same source atom, contradicting forth. Write F({x})={q(x)}. Forth gives q[A]⊆F(A); lifting each {y} with y∈F(A) by back and using an atom of the resulting intersection gives the reverse inclusion. Hence q is uniquely determined and onto. For the converse, q⁻¹[C] witnesses back for every C meeting q[A], with no selection of a family of representatives. Direct images preserve identities and composition, and the finite count follows by partitioning the domain into labeled nonempty fibers. The bundled verify.py was inspected, not executed; it checks labeled maps for seven finite size-pairs and is not needed for the arbitrary-set proof.

evidence: The binary theorem says every bounded morphism into the full frame on {0,1} is uniquely induced by a surjective coloring. For every y in a target Y with at least two atoms, the function p_y sending y to 1 and all others to 0 is onto; its direct image is bounded by the elementary inverse-image witness for back.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Compose F with each p_y direct image. By the binary theorem each composite sends singletons to singletons, so the projections force F({x})={q(x)}. On any A, each binary theorem says that 1 is in the composite image iff it occurs on a singleton from A; equivalently y∈F(A) iff some x∈A has q(x)=y. Each induced binary coloring is onto, so q hits every y. The one-atom target is automatic. This derives the arbitrary-target theorem and its categorical/counting corollaries, without relying on any assumed priority order of the same-day entries.

value.rationale: The classification addresses a natural structural question: whether the full overlap relation permits bounded maps beyond those coming from atom maps. Its choice-free necessary-and-sufficient answer for arbitrary sets is useful for recognizing the morphism category. The standard finite surjection count alone would not merit credit.
